items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: Well the elastic approach to the time I think I would credit Bill Evans and Paul Motian and Scott LaFaro for that kind of free, open-it-up freedom

ctx.x: I heard you probably in around 1968 or so, with Charles Lloyd. And I’d had a couple of — I’ll call them epiphanies now but that was another one. This was in Rochester in some hall, and I think it was the first time I’d heard drummers and bassists really — I’ll call it playing with the time. Not straight ahead but a little bit of elastic approach to the time.

Well the elastic approach to the time I think I would credit Bill Evans and Paul Motian and Scott LaFaro for that kind of free, open-it-up freedom for each individual to be playing collectively but have an equal input. And so after that “Live at the Village Vanguard” you know it kind of just spread throughout the jazz community. So you know you could break time up. Break it up. And then go into the time later. But for coloring it really opened that up.

Is it possible to feel the time — I’m thinking of Latin music with the clave that is almost always there but sometimes no one’s playing it. So I guess I’m trying to relate that to a jazz situation where everybody’s feeling it but — I can’t quite finish this question but it’s an interesting thing to observe and hear when the time is there but no one is enforcing it regularly.

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I like the way Paul's concept of time and space, and color in the music.

ctx.x: Right, that would have been Sunny playing with them. How about Dennis Charles? Because he played with Cecil in the late 50's but I can't recall whether or not he was playing...

You know Dennis, I haven't listened to enough of Dennis to… what I did hear was really great but I'd like if I had the time to go back and listen to some of his work. The other drummer who knocked me out… he might have come later was Paul Motian; in terms of his way of freeing up the rhythm. I mean he could play time really well but you hear in a lot more of his work especially like with Keith and his quartet; you hear Paul kind of has a way of just hitting the drums and playing certain ways. Certain sounds that…
